value: AUROC and AUPRC differ only in how they weight false positives: AUROC weighs all equally, AUPRC weighs them by the inverse of the model's rate of scoring above the threshold, so AUPRC prioritizes correcting high-score errors and, for a model calibrated on a low-prevalence subgroup, favors the higher-prevalence subgroup; AUPRC is therefore not generally the better metric under class imbalance
provenance: mcdermott-2025-closer-look-auroc-auprc-under (arXiv:2401.06091v4, NeurIPS 2024), p.2 Theorem 1; p.4 Theorem 2; p.5 Theorem 3; p.8
certainty_reasons: Started HIGH: theorems with proofs. The subgroup result (Theorem 3) assumes perfect calibration, which the authors name as its largest limitation (p.10); the real-data effect is mild at prevalence ratios up to 2.7 (p.8)

value: Any parameterized quantum circuit built on a real-valued amplitude encoding of the data (including probability loading), with a data-independent ansatz and any observable, computes a function of the form c(x)^T A c(x) with A a real symmetric matrix: the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the kernel (c(x)^T c(x'))^2, which a classical kernel machine computes in O(N^2) time; such models offer no quantum advantage of that kind
